chapter_summary:
As you progress with Ansible automation, especially in a Red Hat Certified Engineer context, you'll find that simple playbooks can quickly become unwieldy and difficult to maintain. Imagine a playbook that configures a web server, a database, and a monitoring agent – it would be hundreds of lines long, repetitive, and hard to debug. This is where Ansible roles become indispensable. Roles provide a standardized, reusable, and self-contained way to organize your automation content. They allow you to break down complex automation tasks into logical, manageable units, promoting modularity, reusability, and easier collaboration within teams. Think of a role as a blueprint for a specific component or service, encapsulating all the necessary tasks, variables, templates, and files required to configure it.

The primary benefit of roles is their ability to enforce a consistent directory structure. When you create a role, Ansible expects specific subdirectories, each serving a distinct purpose. For instance, the `tasks` directory contains the main playbook files (e.g., `main.yml`) that define the actions to be performed. The `handlers` directory holds tasks that are only triggered when notified by other tasks, typically for service restarts or reloads. `templates` is where Jinja2 template files reside, used for generating configuration files dynamically. `files` stores static files that need to be copied to target hosts without modification. `vars` contains role-specific variables, while `defaults` provides default values for variables that can be overridden. `meta` holds metadata about the role, including dependencies and author information. This standardized structure makes it easy for anyone familiar with Ansible to understand and navigate a role, regardless of who created it.

To get started with roles, the `ansible-galaxy` command-line tool is your best friend. It's used for managing Ansible content, including creating new roles, installing roles from Ansible Galaxy (a hub for community-contributed roles), and even packaging your own roles for distribution. When you run `ansible-galaxy init my_webserver_role`, Ansible creates a new directory named `my_webserver_role` with the complete, standard role structure already in place. This saves you the effort of manually creating each subdirectory and ensures consistency. Once the structure is there, you populate the relevant directories. For example, in `my_webserver_role/tasks/main.yml`, you might define tasks to install the Nginx package, ensure the service is running, and copy a configuration file. In `my_webserver_role/templates/nginx.conf.j2`, you'd place the Nginx configuration template, possibly using Jinja2 variables to customize settings based on the target host.

Applying a role to your target hosts is straightforward. Instead of listing individual tasks in your playbook, you simply reference the role. A typical playbook might look like this:

```yaml
---
- name: Deploy web server with Nginx role
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  roles:
    - my_webserver_role
```

In this example, the `webservers` group in your inventory will have the `my_webserver_role` applied to them. Ansible automatically looks for the role in predefined paths (or paths specified in `ansible.cfg`), executes the `tasks/main.yml`, and then processes any handlers, templates, or files as defined within the role.

Understanding variable precedence is crucial when working with roles. Ansible has a well-defined order of precedence for variables, and roles introduce their own layers. Generally, variables defined in `defaults/main.yml` within a role have the lowest precedence, meaning they can be easily overridden. This is ideal for providing sensible defaults that users can customize. Variables in `vars/main.yml` within a role have higher precedence than defaults but can still be overridden by variables defined directly in the playbook, host variables, or group variables. The highest precedence typically comes from extra variables passed via the command line (`-e "key=value"`). A common mistake is to define a variable in `defaults` expecting it to be immutable, only to find it overridden by a group variable. Always remember that `defaults` are meant to be easily overridden, while `vars` are more specific to the role itself but still subject to higher-precedence variables. For RHCE, you must be adept at managing these variable layers to ensure your automation behaves predictably across different environments.

Another important aspect is idempotency. Roles, like all good Ansible content, should be idempotent. This means running a role multiple times should result in the same system state without causing unintended side effects after the first successful run. For instance, a task to install a package should only install it if it's not already present. If it's already installed, the task should report "ok" without making changes. This is fundamental for reliable automation and is a core principle you should adhere to when designing your roles.

screens.title: Understanding and Implementing Ansible Roles
screens.subtitle: Structure, create, and apply reusable automation with roles

narration.text: As your automation grows, single playbooks become hard to read and maintain. In this lesson we treat roles as the practical solution: a role is a self-contained blueprint for a single component or service. You will learn why roles matter for modularity and team collaboration, how Ansible enforces a predictable directory structure, and how to use ansible-galaxy to scaffold roles quickly. We'll also cover how to apply a role from a playbook, how role variables interact with other variable sources, and why idempotency is essential so repeated runs don't break systems. A concrete example we will use throughout is a simple webserver role that installs Nginx, deploys a templated configuration, and restarts the service via a handler. Expect hands-on steps: initialize a role, add tasks and templates, set defaults, and run a playbook that overrides a default port. Common mistakes you will avoid include putting mutable defaults where they should be overridden and assuming role vars cannot be superseded. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to design, run, and reason about roles with predictable behavior and safe variable management.

keyIdea.title: Why roles?
keyIdea.text: Roles make complex automation modular, reusable, and easier to maintain across projects and teams.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map directly to practical skills you will use on RHEL systems. First, you'll explain why roles exist and how they turn sprawling playbooks into modular blueprints that teams can share. Second, you'll identify each standard subdirectory in a role and be able to say what type of content belongs in tasks, handlers, templates, files, vars, defaults, and meta. Third, you'll create a new role using ansible-galaxy init so you never have to handcraft the folder layout. Fourth, you will implement a playbook that applies a custom role to a host group and override defaults when needed. Each objective is tied to an applied step: scaffold the role, add tasks and a template, define defaults, add a handler that restarts a service, and run the playbook against a webservers group. Along the way you will see examples and avoid common errors, like placing an easily overridden value into vars instead of defaults. By the end you will be prepared to build maintainable roles that follow Ansible conventions and behave reliably in test and production.

screens.title: Why use roles? From messy playbooks to modular automation
screens.subtitle: Understand the motivation and practical benefits of roles

narration.text: A role is a standardized, reusable, and self-contained unit of Ansible content that groups tasks, handlers, templates, files, and variables for a single concern. The main benefit is modularity: instead of a single large playbook that mixes unrelated steps, roles let you isolate an operating concern—like configuring a web server—into a blueprint you can reuse across projects. For example, a webserver role encapsulates the package installation, a templated configuration, a handler to restart the service, and defaults for ports. This organization aids collaboration because any engineer familiar with roles can quickly find where templates or handlers live. A common misconception is that roles add extra complexity; in reality, they impose a predictable structure that reduces cognitive load as automation grows. Another mistake is to over-split trivial tasks into too many tiny roles; balance is necessary. Practically, roles enable reuse: call the same role from multiple playbooks with different variables. Key takeaway: roles turn sprawling automation into composable building blocks, making it easier to test, version, and maintain your configuration across environments. How would you split your existing monolithic playbook into logical roles?

keyIdea.title: Modularity and reuse
keyIdea.text: Roles convert large, repetitive playbooks into focused, reusable blueprints for single components like a web server.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Why use roles?
Definition and claim

A role groups the files necessary to configure one concern so you can reuse and share automation consistently. It enforces a directory structure that tells you where to find tasks, templates, handlers, and variables.

Concrete example
An nginx webserver role that installs the package, deploys a templated config using a role variable for the port, and notifies a handler to restart the service.
Common misconception
Some think roles complicate small projects. In practice, they provide clarity as automation grows—use them when a set of tasks is meaningfully reusable.
Key takeaway
Prefer a role when tasks, templates, and handlers naturally belong together and will be reused or maintained by others.
Role in practice
# Example conceptual snippet for a webserver role
- name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
  ansible.builtin.dnf:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Copy Nginx configuration template
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  notify: Restart Nginx

- name: Ensure Nginx service is running
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: true
Ask yourself: is this set of tasks specific to one service and likely to be reused? If yes, it should be a role.

screens.title: Role directory structure
screens.subtitle: What belongs in tasks, handlers, templates, files, vars, defaults, and meta

narration.text: Ansible enforces a predictable directory layout so anyone can open a role and immediately find what they need. The essential folders are tasks, handlers, templates, files, vars, defaults, and meta. Tasks holds the main YAML that performs changes; typically tasks/main. yml drives the role. Handlers contains tasks triggered by notify, like restarting a service. Templates store Jinja2 files used to render configuration based on variables. Files is for static artifacts copied without processing. Defaults/main. yml defines default variables for the role and intentionally has the lowest precedence so playbooks or inventories can override them. Vars/main. yml defines role-specific variables with higher precedence than defaults but lower than extra vars. Meta includes role metadata and dependencies on other roles. A concrete example: put nginx. conf. j2 in templates, a static index. html in files, the install and service tasks in tasks/main. yml, the restart step in handlers/main. yml, and nginx_port in defaults/main. yml. A common error is putting environment-specific values into defaults and later being surprised when group variables override them; remember defaults are meant to be safely overridden. The core insight: the layout separates concerns and makes roles discoverable and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Predictable layout
keyIdea.text: Each subdirectory has a distinct purpose—follow the convention so roles remain understandable and reusable.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Role structure
Role hierarchy and purpose
tasks/
Main actions that change system state. Typically contains main.yml which drives the role.
handlers/
Tasks triggered by notify to perform actions such as restarting services after a configuration change.
templates/ & files/
templates hold Jinja2 for dynamic config; files hold static assets copied as-is.
defaults/ & vars/
defaults/main.yml: lowest precedence sensible defaults. vars/main.yml: role-specific variables with higher precedence than defaults.
meta/
Role metadata and dependency declarations for composition of roles.
Concrete layout example
webserver/
├─ defaults/main.yml   # nginx_port: 80
├─ vars/main.yml       # role-specific values
├─ tasks/main.yml      # install, template, service
├─ handlers/main.yml   # Restart Nginx
├─ templates/nginx.conf.j2
├─ files/index.html
└─ meta/main.yml       # dependencies
Misconception check: defaults are intentionally low precedence. If you need a value to be hard to override, place it in vars, but remember playbook and extra vars can still supersede.

screens.title: Ansible Galaxy: scaffolding a new role
screens.subtitle: Use ansible-galaxy init to create a role skeleton and populate it

narration.text: The fastest way to start a role is ansible-galaxy init. That command creates the full, standard role layout so you don't have to create directories manually. Run ansible-galaxy init webserver and inspect the generated subfolders. Populate tasks/main. yml with installation, template deployment, and service management. Place nginx. conf. j2 in templates and defaults/main. yml to set nginx_port: 80. A concrete walkthrough: after init, open tasks/main. yml and add the ensure package, template, and service tasks. Then add a handler in handlers/main. yml that restarts Nginx and listens for the notify from the template task. A common mistake is to forget to name the handler the same as the notify, or to use a handler name in notify that the handlers file does not define. Another pitfall is editing the wrong file path if ansible-galaxy created the role in a different working directory. The command saves time and enforces consistency. Try it, inspect the skeleton, then add the example task and handler. Finally, commit the role layout to version control so the structure is preserved and discoverable by the team. Ansible Galaxy: scaffolding a new role means ansible-galaxy init creates the canonical role structure so you can focus on content, not folders.. In practical terms, use ansible-galaxy init to create a role skeleton and populate it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scaffold fast
keyIdea.text: ansible-galaxy init creates the canonical role structure so you can focus on content, not folders.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›ansible-galaxy init
Command and quick check
$ ansible-galaxy init webserver
# Creates webserver/ with defaults, tasks, handlers, templates, files, vars, meta
After creating the skeleton, edit tasks/main.yml and handlers/main.yml. Place templates in templates/ and defaults in defaults/main.yml. Commit the role to a repo so teammates can reuse it.
Populate tasks example
---
- name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
  ansible.builtin.dnf:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Copy Nginx configuration template
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  notify: Restart Nginx

- name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: true
Misstep to avoid: notify must match a handler name exactly. Verify handlers/main.yml contains the matching Restart Nginx handler.

screens.title: Templates and handlers in practice
screens.subtitle: Render configuration with Jinja2 and trigger service restarts safely

narration.text: Templates let you generate configuration files dynamically using role variables. In the provided webserver example, nginx. conf. j2 uses a role variable for the listen port and includes the host name. When a template task changes the rendered file, it should notify a handler to restart or reload the service. This pattern ensures the restart happens only when content actually changed, preserving idempotency. For example, the template task notifies Restart Nginx; handlers/main. yml defines the Restart Nginx handler which restarts the service. A common misconception is to restart services unconditionally inside tasks; that breaks idempotency and may cause unnecessary service restarts. Another pitfall is placing dynamic data into files/ instead of templates; files are copied verbatim and cannot render variables. A concrete example is the nginx. conf. j2 that uses {{ nginx_port | default(80) }} and {{ ansible_hostname }} to render a valid config per host. After a run, if no changes are needed the template reports ok and the handler is not called. The core practice: render templates for host-specific configs and use notify/listen to trigger handlers only on real changes.

keyIdea.title: Notify handlers
keyIdea.text: Use templates for variable-driven configs and notify a handler to restart services only when the template actually changes.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Templates & Handlers
Template example (Jinja2)
user  nginx;
worker_processes  auto;

http {
  server {
    listen       {{ nginx_port | default(80) }};
    server_name  {{ ansible_hostname }};
    root         /usr/share/nginx/html;
  }
}
When this file changes after rendering, the template task should use notify: Restart Nginx so the handlers file can restart the service once after all tasks complete.
Handler example
---
- name: Restart Nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
  listen: "Restart Nginx"
Misconception check: do not restart the service inside the template task. Use a handler so the restart runs only when a change occurred and runs once even if multiple tasks notify it.

screens.title: defaults vs vars vs playbook/inventory variables
screens.subtitle: Understand variable precedence with practical examples

narration.text: Variable precedence determines which value Ansible uses when the same key appears in multiple places. In roles, defaults/main. yml holds values with the lowest precedence; they are meant to be easily overridden. Vars/main. yml in a role has higher precedence than defaults but can still be overridden by inventory, playbook, or extra variables. Playbook variables and host/group variables take precedence over role defaults and vars as appropriate, and extra vars passed on the command line have the highest precedence. A clear example: if defaults/main. yml sets nginx_port: 80, the playbook can set nginx_port: 8080 to override that value for the run. If an inventory host variable sets nginx_port to 8090, the highest precedence between playbook and inventory determines the outcome, but extra vars -e "nginx_port=8111" will win. A common error is assuming defaults are fixed; they are intentionally low-precedence. Another mistake is defining many values in vars when you want them easily tunable—then move them to defaults. Takeaway: choose defaults for overridable settings and be deliberate when promoting a variable to a higher-precedence location. Which variable source will you use to make a change overrideable by the team?

keyIdea.title: Precedence matters
keyIdea.text: Defaults are lowest; extra vars are highest. Place values according to how easily they should be overridden.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Variable precedence
Precedence snapshot
defaults/main.yml (lowest)
vars/main.yml (role-specific)
host_vars / group_vars
playbook vars
extra vars (-e) (highest)
Concrete example: defaults sets nginx_port: 80. In deploy_web.yml you can override it with nginx_port: 8080. An extra var passed with -e will override both.
Example scenario
# defaults/main.yml
nginx_port: 80

# playbook override
defaults:
  nginx_port: 8080

# command-line override
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory deploy_web.yml -e "nginx_port=8111"
Misconception check: defaults are not immutable. Use defaults when you want sensible values that the operator can easily change.

screens.title: Applying a role from a playbook
screens.subtitle: How Ansible finds and executes a role when you list it under roles:

narration.text: Applying a role from a playbook is straightforward and concise. Instead of enumerating each task, you reference the role under roles:. Ansible looks for the role in the configured role paths, loads defaults, vars, tasks/main. yml, handlers, templates, and files in a defined order, and executes the tasks. For example, a minimal playbook to deploy a webserver role looks like: hosts: webservers, become: yes, roles: - webserver. If the playbook sets nginx_port, that value overrides the role default. A practical walkthrough: run the playbook against an inventory group webservers that points to your RHEL hosts; Ansible loads the webserver role and processes the template, which may notify Restart Nginx. An important misconception to avoid is assuming that simply placing a role directory alongside a playbook makes it discoverable; ensure roles_path or the local roles directory is correct. Another potential error is forgetting to become when installing packages that require root. The key operational insight: roles let you encapsulate behavior and invoke it with a single line in the playbook, simplifying reuse and clarity. After you run the playbook, verify the service status and configuration to confirm the role applied correctly.

keyIdea.title: Invoke a role
keyIdea.text: List the role under roles: in a playbook and Ansible will execute the role's defaults, tasks, handlers, and templates in order.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Apply role
Playbook example
---
- name: Deploy web server
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  roles:
    - webserver
  vars:
    nginx_port: 8080
Run ansible-playbook -i inventory deploy_web.yml to apply the role. Confirm Nginx is running and that the rendered config uses the overridden port.
Execution flow
  1. Find role in roles_path
  2. Load defaults/main.yml
  3. Load vars/main.yml
  4. Execute tasks/main.yml and notify handlers if needed
  5. Run handlers at end of play
Misconception check: Ensure the role path is configured or the role resides in a roles/ folder adjacent to your playbook. Otherwise Ansible may not locate it.

screens.title: Idempotency: design roles that are safe to run repeatedly
screens.subtitle: Why idempotency matters and how to achieve it

narration.text: Idempotency means running the same automation multiple times leads to the same system state as running it once. In practice, idempotent tasks report ok when no changes are required and only perform changes when necessary. For roles, that means package installation should use state: present so packages are installed only if missing, templates should use the template module which detects content changes before overwriting files, and service management should use state: started or restarted only when notified. A common mistake is to perform unconditional actions such as always copying files without checking differences or always restarting services even when configuration didn't change. That breaks repeatability and can disrupt production services. A concrete check: run your webserver role twice; the second run should show most tasks as ok and not produce service restarts. Also ensure handlers are configured so restarts happen only when needed. Idempotency is foundational in automation because it allows safe, repeatable deployments and simplifies debugging and rollback. Ask yourself: does each task avoid unnecessary changes, and would a second run leave the system unchanged? Idempotency: design roles that are safe to run repeatedly means design tasks so repeated executions don't change the system after the desired state is reached.. In practical terms, why idempotency matters and how to achieve it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Repeatable runs
keyIdea.text: Design tasks so repeated executions don't change the system after the desired state is reached.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Idempotency
Idempotency checklist
  • Use package modules with state: present so installation is conditional.
  • Use template to render files; it will only change when content differs.
  • Notify handlers instead of restarting services inside tasks.
  • Write assertions or checks when performing destructive changes.
Key Takeaway

Make runs safe: repeated plays should not cause unintended changes or service interruptions.

Quick test
# Run twice and compare output $ ansible-playbook -i inventory deploy_web.yml # Run again; most tasks should show 'ok' and handlers should not run if nothing changed
Misconception check: idempotency is not only about modules; it's about designing the role's control flow and notifications to avoid unnecessary change actions.

screens.title: Build the webserver role — step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Follow the provided activity to scaffold, populate, and run the role

narration.text: This guided activity walks through the exact steps from the chapter. Step one: initialize a role with ansible-galaxy init webserver. Inspect the folders that appear. Step two: edit webserver/tasks/main. yml and add tasks to install nginx, render the nginx. conf. j2 template, and ensure the service runs and is enabled. Step three: create webserver/templates/nginx. conf. j2 using a role variable for the port, for example nginx_port with a default of 80. Step four: add defaults/main. yml with nginx_port: 80. Step five: create handlers/main. yml with a Restart Nginx handler that restarts the service when notified. Step six: place any static index. html in files/ if desired. Step seven: write deploy_web. yml next to the role and reference the role in roles:. Optionally override nginx_port in the playbook with 8080 to see the override take effect. Finally, run ansible-playbook -i inventory deploy_web. yml and verify the service with systemctl status nginx or curl localhost:8080. A typical mistake is forgetting to use become: yes for package installation; ensure privilege escalation is enabled. This activity reinforces scaffolding, templates, handlers, variable defaults, and playbook application.

keyIdea.title: Lab walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Scaffold the role, add tasks and templates, set defaults and handlers, and run the playbook to confirm Nginx is configured and running.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step commands and snippets
# 1. Scaffold
ansible-galaxy init webserver

# 2. Populate tasks/main.yml (add install, template, service)
# 3. Create templates/nginx.conf.j2 with {{ nginx_port | default(80) }}

# 4. defaults/main.yml
---
nginx_port: 80

# 5. handlers/main.yml
---
- name: Restart Nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
Remember to commit the role directory and ensure your inventory defines the webservers group pointing to a RHEL host.
Run and verify
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory deploy_web.yml # Verify on target: $ systemctl status nginx $ curl localhost:8080
Common error: missing become: yes in the playbook will prevent package installation. Add become where necessary.

screens.title: Variable-related pitfalls and troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Diagnose why a value didn't change or why a role ignored your setting

narration.text: When a variable doesn't have the value you expect, the most frequent cause is precedence: a higher-precedence variable is overriding the one you set. Start troubleshooting by checking defaults/main. yml in the role, then vars/main. yml, then inventory host/group variables, then playbook vars, and finally extra vars. Use debug tasks in a playbook to print variable values during a run for a specific host. Another typical issue is placing a variable in vars when you intended it to be easily overridden; move it to defaults if you'd like operators to change it. Handlers not running can come from mismatched notify and handler names or from the template reporting no change. If a template is not rendering the expected value, confirm the variable name matches and that the variable is defined in an accessible scope. Always confirm roles_path and file locations if Ansible cannot find a role. The troubleshooting pattern: inspect variable sources in precedence order, add debug statements, verify role location, and check handler names. Closing question: which source should you check first when your intended default is not taking effect?

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot with precedence
keyIdea.text: Check variable sources in order and use debug output to confirm which value Ansible is using at runtime.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.1›Troubleshooting
Diagnostic steps
  1. Check defaults/main.yml for the role's default value.
  2. Check vars/main.yml for role-specific overrides.
  3. Inspect host_vars and group_vars for inventory overrides.
  4. Check playbook vars and command-line extra vars (-e).
  5. Use a debug task to print the value on the target host.
Example debug task:
- name: Show nginx_port debug ansible.builtin.debug: var: nginx_port
Common root causes
  • Mismatched handler and notify names.
  • Placing overridable settings in vars instead of defaults.
  • Role not in roles_path or wrong directory layout.
Misconception check: setting a value in defaults does not prevent later overrides; defaults are intentionally low-precedence.

narration.text: These are the concise ideas to carry forward. First, an Ansible role is a standardized, reusable package that groups tasks, handlers, templates, files, and variables for a single responsibility. Second, ansible-galaxy is the tool to quickly scaffold a role skeleton so you can focus on content. Third, the role directory structure—tasks, handlers, templates, files, vars, defaults, meta—establishes where to put each type of content so others can understand and reuse your work. Keep these central concepts in mind as you design automation: structure matters, tooling accelerates consistency, and discoverability improves collaboration. narration.text: A few more concise reminders: defaults/main. yml provides the lowest-precedence values so operators can override them; vars/main. yml is higher precedence and better for role-internal constants. Idempotency ensures the same play run repeatedly yields the same state and avoids unnecessary restarts. Finally, handlers should be triggered by notify and defined so services restart only when configuration actually changed. Keep these principles in mind as you design and apply roles to RHEL systems for reliable automation. defaults/main.yml
Lowest precedence defaults suitable for environment overrides.
vars/main.yml
Role-specific values with higher precedence than defaults but lower than extra vars.
Idempotency
Ensure tasks and handlers run only when necessary so repeated runs are safe.
Final thought

Structure, consistent defaults, and idempotent design together keep automation predictable and maintainable across environments.
